title: Αἴας καὶ Ἕκτωρ
titleEn: Two Rallying Speeches and the Fall of Dolops — Iliad 15.471–558
part: Two Rallying Speeches and the Fall of Dolops (15.471–558)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Ajax tells Teucer to leave his useless bow and fight with spear and shield, and Teucer arms and comes to his side. Hector, seeing Teucer’s missiles made useless, rallies the Trojans and Lycians: the might of Zeus is plain to men, and to die defending one’s country is no shame. Ajax answers with a speech of his own to the Argives: now they must be saved or perish, and there is no better course than close fighting. Then the killing begins. Hector kills Schedius and Ajax Laodamas, and Polydamas kills Otus; Meges, rushing at Polydamas, is turned from him by Apollo and kills Croesmus. Dolops, a strong spearman, strikes Meges’ shield, but the breastplate his father brought home saves him. Meges cuts the crest from Dolops’ helmet, and Menelaus comes up unseen and spears Dolops in the back. Hector rebukes Melanippus, Dolops’ cousin, and calls him to the fight.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita megas Telamōnios Aias·
sentences.l: Him then answered great Telamonian Ajax:
sentences.i: Then great Telamonian Ajax answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is Teucer, whose bowstring Zeus has just broken, and ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, with its ending elided. The line is the usual reply formula, here with μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας ‘great Telamonian Ajax’; the adjective tells this Ajax, the son of Telamon, from the other Ajax, the son of Oileus. The part opens in the middle of the exchange, straight after Teucer’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπον ἀλλὰ βιὸν μὲν ἔα καὶ ταρφέας ἰοὺς
κεῖσθαι, ἐπεὶ συνέχευε θεὸς Δαναοῖσι μεγήρας·
sentences.tr:
ō pepon alla bion men ea kai tarpheas ious
keisthai, epei synecheue theos Danaoisi megēras·
sentences.l:
“O good one, but the bow indeed allow, and the thick arrows,
to lie, since a god has confounded everything, begrudging the Danaans;
sentences.i: “My good fellow, let your bow lie, and your many arrows, since a god has thrown everything into confusion, begrudging the Danaans;
sentences.n: Ajax speaks to Teucer. ὦ πέπον is a form of address, ‘my good fellow’, whose exact meaning is not known; the tone here is friendly. ἔα is the present imperative of ἐάω ‘allow, let be’, and its objects βιόν ‘bow’ (the accent tells it from βίος ‘life’) and ταρφέας ἰούς ‘thick arrows’ (ταρφύς ‘thick, crowded’) go with κεῖσθαι ‘to lie’. συνέχευε is the aorist of συγχέω ‘pour together, confound’ and has no stated object, so the English supplies ‘everything’; it points back at what has just happened to the bow. θεός is an unnamed god, and μεγήρας is the aorist participle of μεγαίρω ‘begrudge’, with Δαναοῖσι the epic dative plural ‘the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ χερσὶν ἑλὼν δολιχὸν δόρυ καὶ σάκος ὤμῳ
μάρναό τε Τρώεσσι καὶ ἄλλους ὄρνυθι λαούς.
sentences.tr:
autar chersin helōn dolichon dory kai sakos ōmōi
marnao te Trōessi kai allous ornythi laous.
sentences.l:
but with your hands taking a long spear and a shield on your shoulder
fight against the Trojans, and rouse the other people.
sentences.i: but take a long spear in your hands and a shield on your shoulder, and fight the Trojans, and rouse the rest of the people.
sentences.n: The bowman is told to become a spearman. χερσὶν ἑλών is ‘taking in your hands’ (the aorist participle of αἱρέω), δολιχὸν δόρυ ‘a long spear’, and σάκος ὤμῳ ‘a shield on your shoulder’, with ὤμῳ the dative singular of ὦμος. μάρναο is the imperative of μάρναμαι ‘fight’ (the ending -αο is the epic form of -ασο), with Τρώεσσι the epic dative plural ‘against the Trojans’. ὄρνυθι is the imperative of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, and ἄλλους … λαούς is ‘the other people’.

sentences.t:
μὴ μὰν ἀσπουδί γε δαμασσάμενοί περ ἕλοιεν
νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους, ἀλλὰ μνησώμεθα χάρμης.
sentences.tr:
mē man aspoudi ge damassamenoi per heloien
nēas eÿsselmous, alla mnēsōmetha charmēs.
sentences.l:
Truly may they not, without trouble, though having subdued us, take
the well-benched ships, but let us be mindful of the joy of battle.”
sentences.i: May they not take the well-benched ships without trouble, even if they overcome us; but let us remember the joy of battle.”
sentences.n: μὴ μάν ‘truly not’ introduces a wish that the Trojans may not do something, and ἕλοιεν is the aorist optative of αἱρέω ‘take’. ἀσπουδί (ἀ- ‘without’ + σπουδή ‘effort’) is ‘without trouble’, sharpened by γε. δαμασσάμενοί περ is the aorist middle participle of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, with περ ‘even though’: even though they have overcome us. νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους is the stock ‘well-benched ships’. μνησώμεθα is the aorist subjunctive of μιμνῄσκομαι, ‘let us be mindful’, with χάρμης ‘the joy of battle’ in the genitive. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δὲ τόξον μὲν ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν ἔθηκεν,
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι σάκος θέτο τετραθέλυμνον,
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho de toxon men eni klisiēisin ethēken,
autar ho g’ amph’ ōmoisi sakos theto tetrathelymnon,
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he the bow in the huts set down,
but he around his shoulders the shield set, four-layered,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he laid his bow down in the huts, and about his shoulders he set the four-layered shield,
sentences.n: φάθ’ is the unaugmented φάτο ‘he said’, elided before the rough breathing of ὅ. ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Teucer, who now does as he is told, and μέν … αὐτάρ sets his two acts against each other: the bow is put down, the shield taken up. ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν is ‘in the huts’ (κλισίη ‘hut’, the dwellings of the camp), and θέτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of τίθημι, ‘set on (himself)’. τετραθέλυμνον ‘four-layered’ is the Odyssey’s word for this shield, and its meaning is not known. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: δὲ in ὃ δὲ, short by nature, falls on the long place of the second foot and has to be read long.

sentences.t:
κρατὶ δ’ ἐπ’ ἰφθίμῳ κυνέην εὔτυκτον ἔθηκεν
ἵππουριν, δεινὸν δὲ λόφος καθύπερθεν ἔνευεν·
sentences.tr:
krati d’ ep’ iphthimōi kyneēn eutykton ethēken
hippourin, deinon de lophos kathyperthen eneuen·
sentences.l:
and on his mighty head the well-made helmet he placed,
horse-tailed, and fearsomely the crest above nodded;
sentences.i: and on his mighty head he placed the well-made helmet, with its horsetail plume, and fearsomely the crest nodded above;
sentences.n: The two lines are the arming lines of the Odyssey, and the first is also the line for Paris at 3.336, so the English is theirs. κρατί is the dative of κάρη ‘head’, ἰφθίμῳ ‘mighty’, κυνέην ‘helmet’, and εὔτυκτον ‘well-made’; ἵππουριν (ἵππος ‘horse’ + οὐρά ‘tail’) describes the plume of horsehair. δεινόν is adverbial, ‘fearsomely’, and λόφος is the crest, which nodded (ἔνευεν, imperfect of νεύω) above the helmet.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος ἀκαχμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, μάλα δ’ ὦκα θέων Αἴαντι παρέστη.
sentences.tr:
heileto d’ alkimon enchos akachmenon oxeï chalkōi,
bē d’ ienai, mala d’ ōka theōn Aianti parestē.
sentences.l:
and he took up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze,
and set out to go, and very quickly running he stood beside Ajax.
sentences.i: he took up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze, and set out; and running very fast he came to stand beside Ajax.
sentences.n: εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘took up (for himself)’, with ἄλκιμον ἔγχος ‘a sturdy spear’ and ἀκαχμένον ‘pointed’ (a participle, from the root of ἀκή ‘point’); the first line is the one for Nestor’s spear at 10.135, and its English is that line’s. βῆ is the root aorist of βαίνω ‘went’, ἰέναι ‘to go’; μάλα ὦκα is ‘very quickly’, θέων ‘running’ (present participle of θέω), and παρέστη is the aorist of παρίστημι ‘stood beside’, with Αἴαντι in the dative.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὡς εἶδεν Τεύκρου βλαφθέντα βέλεμνα,
Τρωσί τε καὶ Λυκίοισιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ hōs eiden Teukrou blaphthenta belemna,
Trōsi te kai Lykioisin ekekleto makron aÿsas·
sentences.l:
And Hector, when he saw Teucer’s missiles hindered,
to the Trojans and Lycians called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And when Hector saw Teucer’s missiles made useless, he gave orders to the Trojans and Lycians, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: Hector has seen what we have just seen: Teucer’s bowstring has snapped. βλαφθέντα is the aorist passive participle of βλάπτω ‘hinder, harm’, agreeing with βέλεμνα, a plural noun for whatever is shot or thrown, here Teucer’s arrows and bow. The missiles are ‘hindered’, that is, put out of use. Τρωσί τε καὶ Λυκίοισιν is ‘to the Trojans and the Lycians’ (the first with the old dative ending -σι, the second with the epic -οισιν). ἐκέκλετο is the aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘order, urge’, and μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’ is the adverbial μακρόν ‘at length, loudly’ with the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’. The second line stands as it does at 11.285.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Δάρδανοι ἀγχιμαχηταὶ
ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς
νῆας ἀνὰ γλαφυράς·
sentences.tr:
Trōes kai Lykioi kai Dardanoi anchimachētai
aneres este philoi, mnēsasthe de thouridos alkēs
nēas ana glaphyras·
sentences.i: “Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, fighters at close quarters, be men, friends, and remember impetuous might along the hollow ships;
sentences.n: Hector speaks. His first two lines repeat his call at 8.173–174, and the second of them also stands at 6.112. Three peoples are named, and ἀγχιμαχηταί ‘close-fighters’ (ἀγχί ‘near’ + μάχομαι ‘fight’) is the stock epithet of men who fight at close quarters. ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι is ‘be men, friends’, with ἔστε the imperative of εἰμί and ἀνέρες the plural of ἀνήρ with epic ε. μνήσασθε is the aorist imperative middle of μιμνῄσκομαι, ‘be mindful’, with θούριδος ἀλκῆς in the genitive, ‘impetuous might’ (θοῦρις ‘rushing, impetuous’). νῆας ἀνὰ γλαφυράς is ‘along the hollow ships’, ἀνά with the accusative meaning ‘up and along’.

sentences.t:
δὴ γὰρ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
ἀνδρὸς ἀριστῆος Διόθεν βλαφθέντα βέλεμνα.
sentences.tr:
dē gar idon ophthalmoisin
andros aristēos Diothen blaphthenta belemna.
sentences.l:
for indeed I saw with my eyes
the missiles of a best man hindered from Zeus.
sentences.i: for I saw with my own eyes the missiles of one of the best men made useless by Zeus.
sentences.n: ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω ‘saw’, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν the epic dative plural ‘with my eyes’. ἀνδρὸς ἀριστῆος is ‘of a best man’, the epic genitive of ἀριστεύς (plural ἀριστῆες ‘the best men’), and the man is Teucer, who is not named. Διόθεν is ‘from Zeus’, the ending -θεν marking where it comes from, so Hector reads the broken string as Zeus’s doing. βλαφθέντα βέλεμνα repeats the words of line 484.

sentences.t:
ῥεῖα δ’ ἀρίγνωτος Διὸς ἀνδράσι γίγνεται ἀλκή,
ἠμὲν ὁτέοισιν κῦδος ὑπέρτερον ἐγγυαλίξῃ,
sentences.tr:
rheia d’ arignōtos Dios andrasi gignetai alkē,
ēmen hoteoisin kydos hyperteron engyalixēi,
sentences.l:
And easily-known to men becomes the might of Zeus,
both to those to whom he may put greater glory into their hands,
sentences.i: The might of Zeus is easily known to men, both to those into whose hands he puts the greater glory,
sentences.n: The sentence is a general truth. ῥεῖα is ‘easily’, and ἀρίγνωτος ‘easily known’ describes ἀλκή ‘might’, with Διός in the genitive ‘of Zeus’ and ἀνδράσι ‘to men’. ἠμέν … ἠδέ (the next line) is ‘both … and’. ὁτέοισιν is the epic dative plural of ὅστις ‘to those to whom’, κῦδος ὑπέρτερον is ‘greater glory’, and ἐγγυαλίξῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐγγυαλίζω ‘put into the hands’, a general ‘whenever he puts’.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὅτινας μινύθῃ τε καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλῃσιν ἀμύνειν,
ὡς νῦν Ἀργείων μινύθει μένος, ἄμμι δ’ ἀρήγει.
sentences.tr:
ēd’ hotinas minythēi te kai ouk ethelēisin amynein,
hōs nyn Argeiōn minythei menos, ammi d’ arēgei.
sentences.l:
and those whom he lessens and does not wish to defend,
as now of the Argives he lessens the might, and us he helps.
sentences.i: and to those whom he lessens and is unwilling to defend, as now he lessens the might of the Argives and helps us.
sentences.n: ἠδ’ ὅτινας is ‘and those whom’, the second half of the pair begun in the last line, and the subject throughout is Zeus. μινύθῃ is the subjunctive of μινύθω in its transitive sense ‘lessen, diminish’, and in the next line μινύθει is the same verb, in the indicative, with μένος ‘might’ as its object. οὐκ ἐθέλῃσιν ἀμύνειν is ‘does not wish to defend’ (ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, here to ward off harm from someone). ἄμμι is the epic dative ‘for us’, and ἀρήγει ‘helps’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μάχεσθ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἀολλέες·
sentences.tr: alla machesth’ epi nēusin aollees·
sentences.l: But fight at the ships in a close mass;
sentences.i: But fight at the ships in a close mass;
sentences.n: μάχεσθ’ is the imperative of μάχομαι ‘fight’ with its ending elided, and νηυσὶν the epic dative plural of ναῦς ‘ships’. ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ (ἀολλής ‘crowded together’) is nominative plural, agreeing with the men Hector addresses.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κεν ὑμέων
βλήμενος ἠὲ τυπεὶς θάνατον καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ
τεθνάτω·
sentences.tr:
hos de ken hymeōn
blēmenos ēe typeis thanaton kai potmon epispēi
tethnatō·
sentences.i: and whoever among you is hit or struck and meets death and doom, let him be dead;
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κεν … ἐπίσπῃ is a general ‘and whoever … meets’, with κεν and the aorist subjunctive. ὑμέων is the epic genitive plural of σύ ‘of you’. βλήμενος is the epic aorist middle participle of βάλλω, ‘hit’ by a missile, and τυπείς the aorist passive participle of τύπτω ‘struck’. θάνατον καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ is ‘meets death and doom’ (ἐπισπεῖν ‘come upon, meet’). τεθνάτω is the perfect imperative of θνῄσκω, ‘let him be dead’: the perfect gives the state, not the dying.

sentences.t:
οὔ οἱ ἀεικὲς ἀμυνομένῳ περὶ πάτρης
τεθνάμεν·
sentences.tr:
ou hoi aeikes amynomenōi peri patrēs
tethnamen·
sentences.l:
for him it is not unseemly, defending, for his fatherland,
to be dead;
sentences.i: it is no unseemly thing for him to be dead in defence of his fatherland;
sentences.n: οὔ οἱ ἀεικές is ‘it is not unseemly for him’, with οἱ the dative ‘for him’, ἀεικές ‘unseemly’, and ἐστί understood. ἀμυνομένῳ is the present middle participle of ἀμύνω ‘defend’, agreeing with οἱ, and περὶ πάτρης is ‘for his fatherland’ (πάτρη, the poetic form of πατρίς). τεθνάμεν is the perfect infinitive of θνῄσκω, ‘to be dead’ (Attic τεθνάναι).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄλοχός τε σόη καὶ παῖδες ὀπίσσω,
καὶ οἶκος καὶ κλῆρος ἀκήρατος, εἴ κεν Ἀχαιοὶ
οἴχωνται σὺν νηυσὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
all’ alochos te soē kai paides opissō,
kai oikos kai klēros akēratos, ei ken Achaioi
oichōntai syn nēusi philēn es patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
but his wife is safe, and his children too hereafter,
and his house and his allotment untouched, if the Achaeans
have gone with their ships to their dear fatherland.”
sentences.i: but his wife will be safe, and his children afterwards, and his house and his allotted land untouched, if the Achaeans have gone back with their ships to their dear fatherland.”
sentences.n: The sentence has no verb; ‘is’ or ‘will be’ must be supplied. ἄλοχος is ‘wife’, σόη the epic form of σῶς ‘safe’, and παῖδες ὀπίσσω ‘children afterwards’ (ὀπίσσω ‘behind, afterwards’, here in time to come). κλῆρος is the plot of land allotted to a family, and ἀκήρατος ‘untouched’. εἴ κεν … οἴχωνται is ‘if the Achaeans go off’ (the subjunctive of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’): once the enemy are away, the home stays safe. The last line is the whole of 7.460. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: The line closes a speech by telling its effect, and is the same as 5.470 and 13.155. εἰπών is the aorist participle of εἶπον ‘having spoken’, ὄτρυνε the unaugmented past of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου is ‘the might and the heart of each man’. The speaker is Hector.

sentences.t: Αἴας δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐκέκλετο οἷς ἑτάροισιν·
sentences.tr: Aias d’ auth’ heterōthen ekekleto hois hetaroisin·
sentences.l: And Ajax in turn, on the other side, called out to his own companions:
sentences.i: And Ajax, on the other side in his turn, gave orders to his own companions:
sentences.n: αὖθ’ is the elided αὖτε ‘in turn’, and ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’: Ajax answers Hector’s speech with one of his own on the Achaean side. ἐκέκλετο is the aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘order, urge’, as at 485. οἷς ἑτάροισιν is ‘to his own companions’: οἷς is the possessive ὅς, ‘his own’, and ἑτάροισιν the dative plural of ἑταῖρος.

sentences.t:
αἰδὼς Ἀργεῖοι· νῦν ἄρκιον ἢ ἀπολέσθαι
ἠὲ σαωθῆναι καὶ ἀπώσασθαι κακὰ νηῶν.
sentences.tr:
aidōs Argeioi· nyn arkion ē apolesthai
ēe saōthēnai kai apōsasthai kaka nēōn.
sentences.l:
“Shame, Argives! Now it is assured, either to perish
or to be saved and to thrust the evils off from the ships.
sentences.i: “Shame, Argives! Now the choice is sure: to perish, or to be saved and drive the evils away from the ships.
sentences.n: Ajax speaks. αἰδώς ‘shame’ is a cry, as at 5.787 and 13.95, calling on the men’s sense of honour. ἄρκιον has its usual sense ‘sufficient, certain’, and with ἐστί understood it means ‘it is assured’; I read it as the choice being settled, ἢ … ἠέ ‘either … or’. ἀπολέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπόλλυμι ‘to perish’ and σαωθῆναι the aorist passive infinitive of σαόω ‘to be saved’. ἀπώσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπωθέω ‘thrust away from oneself’, with κακά ‘evils’ and νηῶν the genitive ‘from the ships’.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἔλπεσθ’ ἢν νῆας ἕλῃ κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
ἐμβαδὸν ἵξεσθαι ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἕκαστος;
sentences.tr:
ē elpesth’ ēn nēas helēi korythaiolos Hektōr
embadon hixesthai hēn patrida gaian hekastos;
sentences.l:
Truly do you expect, if Hector of the glancing helmet takes the ships,
on foot to reach his own fatherland, each man?
sentences.i: Do you really expect, if Hector of the glancing helmet takes the ships, that each of you will go home on foot to his own fatherland?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question, ‘do you really …?’. ἔλπεσθ’ is the second plural of ἔλπομαι ‘expect’, ἢν is ‘if’ (ἐάν) with the aorist subjunctive ἕλῃ ‘takes’, and κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ is the stock ‘Hector of the glancing helmet’. ἐμβαδόν is an adverb ‘on foot’, the point being that with the ships in Hector’s hands the men could not sail home. ἵξεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’, ἣν … πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘his own fatherland’ (ἥν the possessive ὅς), and ἕκαστος ‘each man’ stands last for emphasis.

sentences.t:
ἦ οὐκ ὀτρύνοντος ἀκούετε λαὸν ἅπαντα
Ἕκτορος, ὃς δὴ νῆας ἐνιπρῆσαι μενεαίνει;
sentences.tr:
ē ouk otrynontos akouete laon hapanta
Hektoros, hos dē nēas eniprēsai meneainei;
sentences.l:
Truly do you not hear Hector urging on all the people,
who indeed is eager to set the ships on fire?
sentences.i: Do you really not hear Hector urging on all the people, he who is eager to set the ships on fire?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question again, as at 504, and ἀκούετε takes the genitive ὀτρύνοντος … Ἕκτορος, ‘hear Hector urging on’, with λαὸν ἅπαντα ‘all the people’ as the object of the participle. ὃς δή is ‘who indeed’, νῆας ἐνιπρῆσαι ‘to set the ships on fire’ (the aorist infinitive of ἐνίπρημι), and μενεαίνει ‘is eager’, the present of μενεαίνω.

sentences.t: οὐ μὰν ἔς γε χορὸν κέλετ’ ἐλθέμεν, ἀλλὰ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr: ou man es ge choron kelet’ elthemen, alla machesthai.
sentences.l: Truly not to a dance does he bid them come, but to fight.
sentences.i: It is not to a dance that he bids them come, but to fight.
sentences.n: The sneer is Ajax’s: Hector’s call is a call to work, not to play. οὐ μάν is ‘truly not’, and ἔς … χορόν ‘to a dance’, with γε sharpening the word. κέλετ’ is an elided form of κέλομαι ‘bid’, ἐλθέμεν the epic aorist infinitive of ἔρχομαι ‘to come’ (Attic ἐλθεῖν), and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’.

sentences.t:
ἡμῖν δ’ οὔ τις τοῦδε νόος καὶ μῆτις ἀμείνων
ἢ αὐτοσχεδίῃ μῖξαι χεῖράς τε μένος τε.
sentences.tr:
hēmin d’ ou tis toude noos kai mētis ameinōn
ē autoschediēi mixai cheiras te menos te.
sentences.l:
And for us no mind and cunning is better than this,
than to mingle, at close quarters, hands and might.
sentences.i: And we have no better mind or cunning than this: to bring our hands and our might together at close quarters.
sentences.n: ἡμῖν δ’ οὔ τις is ‘and for us there is no’, νόος καὶ μῆτις ‘mind and cunning’ (as at 7.447), and ἀμείνων ‘better’. τοῦδε is the genitive of comparison ‘than this’, and the ἤ that follows gives the thing compared: the poet states the comparison twice, once with the pronoun and once with the infinitive. αὐτοσχεδίῃ is ‘at close quarters’ (adverbial dative, from the word that gives αὐτοσχεδόν). μῖξαι is the aorist infinitive of μίγνυμι ‘mingle’, and χεῖράς τε μένος τε is ‘hands and might’: to come to blows at full strength.

sentences.t:
βέλτερον ἢ ἀπολέσθαι ἕνα χρόνον ἠὲ βιῶναι
ἢ δηθὰ στρεύγεσθαι ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι
ὧδ’ αὔτως παρὰ νηυσὶν ὑπ’ ἀνδράσι χειροτέροισιν.
sentences.tr:
belteron ē apolesthai hena chronon ēe biōnai
ē dētha streugesthai en ainēi dēïotēti
hōd’ autōs para nēusin hyp’ andrasi cheiroteroisin.
sentences.l:
Better it is either to perish for one time, or to live,
than for a long time to be worn out in dread fighting
so, idly, beside the ships, at the hands of worse men.”
sentences.i: It is better either to die once and for all, or to live, than to be worn out for a long time in dreadful fighting like this, to no purpose, beside the ships, at the hands of worse men.”
sentences.n: βέλτερον is ‘better’ (the epic comparative of ἀγαθός), with ἐστί understood. The first ἤ pairs with ἠέ in ‘either … or’, with the infinitives ἀπολέσθαι ‘to perish’ and βιῶναι ‘to live’ (aorist of βιόω), and ἕνα χρόνον is ‘for one time, once for all’; the second ἤ is ‘than’. στρεύγεσθαι is ‘to be worn out’, δηθά ‘for a long time’, and ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι ‘in dread fighting’ (δηϊοτής ‘hostile fighting’). ὧδ’ αὔτως is ‘just so, idly’, and ὑπ’ ἀνδράσι χειροτέροισιν ‘at the hands of worse men’ (χειρότερος ‘worse, inferior’). The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: The same closing line as at 500, now for Ajax. The two speeches thus end alike, and each side is roused to the same pitch.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ἕκτωρ μὲν ἕλε Σχεδίον Περιμήδεος υἱὸν
ἀρχὸν Φωκήων, Αἴας δ’ ἕλε Λαοδάμαντα
ἡγεμόνα πρυλέων Ἀντήνορος ἀγλαὸν υἱόν·
sentences.tr:
enth’ Hektōr men hele Schedion Perimēdeos huion
archon Phōkēōn, Aias d’ hele Laodamanta
hēgemona pryleōn Antēnoros aglaon huion·
sentences.i: Then Hector killed Schedius, son of Perimedes, commander of the Phocians, and Ajax killed Laodamas, leader of the foot-soldiers, the splendid son of Antenor;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘then’, and ἕλε is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘took’, used here, as often, for taking a man’s life. Each side loses a leader: Hector kills Schedius, a man of the Achaean side, and Ajax kills Laodamas, a Trojan. Σχεδίον Περιμήδεος υἱόν is ‘Schedius, son of Perimedes’ (Περιμήδεος the epic genitive), and ἀρχὸν Φωκήων ‘commander of the Phocians’ (Φωκῆες, a people of central Greece, allies of the Achaeans). ἡγεμόνα πρυλέων is ‘leader of the foot-soldiers’ (πρυλέες ‘foot-soldiers’), and Ἀντήνορος ἀγλαὸν υἱόν ‘Antenor’s splendid son’.

sentences.t:
Πουλυδάμας δ’ Ὦτον Κυλλήνιον ἐξενάριξε
Φυλεΐδεω ἕταρον, μεγαθύμων ἀρχὸν Ἐπειῶν.
sentences.tr:
Poulydamas d’ Ōton Kyllēnion exenarixe
Phyleïdeō hetaron, megathymōn archon Epeiōn.
sentences.l:
And Polydamas despoiled Otus the Cyllenian,
companion of Phyleus’-son, commander of the great-hearted Epeians.
sentences.i: And Polydamas killed and stripped of his armour Otus of Cyllene, a companion of the son of Phyleus and commander of the great-hearted Epeians.
sentences.n: Πουλυδάμας is the Iliad’s spelling of Polydamas, and ἐξενάριξε is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip of armour’. Ὦτον Κυλλήνιον is ‘Otus the Cyllenian’ (of Cyllene, a place in Elis, the Epeians’ land). Φυλεΐδεω is the patronymic of Φυλεύς in the epic genitive -εω, ‘of Phyleus’ son’, and he is Meges, who is named in the next line. ἀρχόν, in the accusative, agrees with Ὦτον, so it is Otus who is ‘commander of the great-hearted Epeians’. μεγαθύμων ‘great-hearted’.

sentences.t: τῷ δὲ Μέγης ἐπόρουσεν ἰδών·
sentences.tr: tōi de Megēs eporousen idōn·
sentences.l: And at him Meges rushed, having seen him;
sentences.i: Meges saw him, and rushed at him;
sentences.n: τῷ ‘at him’ is Polydamas, who has just killed Otus, and Meges is the Phyleid of the last line. ἐπόρουσεν is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush at’, and ἰδών the aorist participle ‘having seen’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕπαιθα λιάσθη
Πουλυδάμας·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hypaitha liasthē
Poulydamas·
sentences.l:
but he bent aside,
Polydamas;
sentences.i: but Polydamas swerved aside;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘but he’ is Polydamas, named at the start of the next line after the verb. ὕπαιθα is ‘aside’, and λιάσθη the aorist passive of λιάζομαι ‘bend, give way’ (the same verb as ἐλιάσθη at 543).

sentences.t:
καὶ τοῦ μὲν ἀπήμβροτεν· οὐ γὰρ Ἀπόλλων
εἴα Πάνθου υἱὸν ἐνὶ προμάχοισι δαμῆναι·
sentences.tr:
kai tou men apēmbroten· ou gar Apollōn
eia Panthou huion eni promachoisi damēnai·
sentences.l:
and him indeed he missed; for Apollo
would not let Panthous’ son be subdued among the foremost fighters;
sentences.i: and Meges missed him; for Apollo would not allow the son of Panthous to be overcome among the foremost fighters;
sentences.n: καὶ τοῦ μέν is ‘and him at least’, and ἀπήμβροτεν is the aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω ‘miss’. Apollo is the reason: he watches over Polydamas. εἴα is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, Πάνθου υἱόν is ‘the son of Panthous’ (Polydamas, as at 13.756), and δαμῆναι the aorist passive infinitive of δαμάζω ‘be subdued’. ἐνὶ προμάχοισι is ‘among the foremost fighters’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γε Κροίσμου στῆθος μέσον οὔτασε δουρί.
sentences.tr: autar ho ge Kroismou stēthos meson outase douri.
sentences.l: but he in the middle of the chest wounded Croesmus with his spear.
sentences.i: but he stabbed Croesmus in the middle of the chest with his spear.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γε ‘but he’ is Meges, who, having missed Polydamas, turns on another man. Κροίσμου is the genitive of Κροῖσμος, with στῆθος μέσον ‘the middle of the chest’ as the part struck (‘Croesmus’ chest, in the middle’), and οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘stab, wound’. δουρί is the epic dative ‘with the spear’.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών· ὃ δ’ ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἐσύλα.
sentences.tr: doupēsen de pesōn· ho d’ ap’ ōmōn teuche’ esyla.
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud; and he from the shoulders was stripping the armour.
sentences.i: Croesmus fell with a thud, and the other was stripping the armour from his shoulders.
sentences.n: δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω ‘thud, fall with a thud’, and πεσών ‘having fallen’. ὃ δ’ is the victor, Meges, who ἐσύλα ‘was stripping’ (the imperfect of συλάω), with ἀπ’ ὤμων ‘from the shoulders’ and τεύχε’ the elided τεύχεα ‘armour’.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ τῷ ἐπόρουσε Δόλοψ αἰχμῆς ἐῢ εἰδὼς
Λαμπετίδης, ὃν Λάμπος ἐγείνατο φέρτατον υἱὸν
Λαομεδοντιάδης εὖ εἰδότα θούριδος ἀλκῆς,
sentences.tr:
tophra de tōi eporouse Dolops aichmēs eÿ eidōs
Lampetidēs, hon Lampos egeinato phertaton huion
Laomedontiadēs eu eidota thouridos alkēs,
sentences.l:
And meanwhile at him rushed Dolops, well knowing the spear,
Lampetus’-son, whom Lampus begot, the best son,
Laomedon’s-son, well knowing impetuous might,
sentences.i: Meanwhile Dolops rushed at him, son of Lampetus, who knew the spear well, whom Lampus, son of Laomedon, begot as his best son, and who knew impetuous might well,
sentences.n: τόφρα δέ is ‘and meanwhile’, and τῷ is Meges. Δόλοψ is the attacker. Λαμπετίδης is a patronymic whose base would be Λάμπετος; the next words name the father as Λάμπος, so the two names seem to be forms of one name, though the poem does not say so. Λάμπος ἐγείνατο is ‘Lampus begot’ (the aorist middle of γείνομαι), Λαομεδοντιάδης ‘son of Laomedon’ is Lampus, and φέρτατον ‘best’ in the sense of strongest. εὖ εἰδότα … θούριδος ἀλκῆς is ‘who knew impetuous might well’, as αἰχμῆς ἐῢ εἰδώς is ‘who knew the spear well’; αἰχμή here means the spear and the fighting with it.

sentences.t:
ὃς τότε Φυλεΐδαο μέσον σάκος οὔτασε δουρὶ
ἐγγύθεν ὁρμηθείς·
sentences.tr:
hos tote Phyleïdao meson sakos outase douri
engythen hormētheis·
sentences.l:
who then thrust at the middle of Phyleus’-son’s shield with a spear,
having rushed from close by;
sentences.i: who then, rushing in from close by, stabbed the middle of the shield of the son of Phyleus with his spear;
sentences.n: ὃς τότε is ‘who then’, and the verb is οὔτασε, a thrust from close at hand (‘stabbed’; here it lands on a shield, so nothing is wounded), with μέσον σάκος ‘the middle of the shield’ and Φυλεΐδαο (the epic genitive -αο) ‘of the son of Phyleus’: Meges. ὁρμηθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω ‘rush’, and ἐγγύθεν ‘from close by’.

sentences.t:
πυκινὸς δέ οἱ ἤρκεσε θώρηξ,
τόν ῥ’ ἐφόρει γυάλοισιν ἀρηρότα·
sentences.tr:
pykinos de hoi ērkese thōrēx,
ton rh’ ephorei gyaloisin arērota·
sentences.l:
and for him the solid breastplate warded it off,
which he was wearing, fitted with hollows;
sentences.i: but the solid breastplate warded it off, the one he was wearing, fitted with its hollow plates;
sentences.n: πυκινὸς … θώρηξ is ‘the solid breastplate’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is Meges, who wears it. ἤρκεσε is the aorist of ἀρκέω ‘ward off, be a defence’. τόν ῥ’ is ‘which’ (τόν used as a relative, ῥ’ for ῥα), and ἐφόρει the imperfect of φορέω ‘wear’. γυάλοισιν is the dative plural of γύαλον ‘hollow’, here the hollowed plates of the breastplate, and ἀρηρότα the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit together’; the exact construction is not certain.

sentences.t:
τόν ποτε Φυλεὺς
ἤγαγεν ἐξ Ἐφύρης, ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος.
sentences.tr:
ton pote Phyleus
ēgagen ex Ephyrēs, potamou apo Sellēentos.
sentences.l:
which once Phyleus brought
from Ephyre, from the river Selleeis.
sentences.i: which Phyleus had once brought from Ephyre, from the river Selleeis.
sentences.n: The breastplate has a history: it is his father’s. τόν is again ‘which’, ποτε ‘once’, and ἤγαγεν the aorist of ἄγω ‘brought’. Ἐφύρης is the genitive ‘from Ephyre’, and ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος is ‘from the river Selleeis’, with ἄπο placed after its noun.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνος γάρ οἱ ἔδωκεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Εὐφήτης
ἐς πόλεμον φορέειν δηΐων ἀνδρῶν ἀλεωρήν·
sentences.tr:
xeinos gar hoi edōken anax andrōn Euphētēs
es polemon phoreein dēïōn andrōn aleōrēn·
sentences.l:
for as his guest-friend gave it to him the lord of men, Euphetes,
to wear into war, a defence from hostile men;
sentences.i: for Euphetes, lord of men, who was his guest-friend, had given it to him to wear into war as a defence against enemy men;
sentences.n: ξεῖνος is a guest-friend, bound to Phyleus by the exchange of hospitality, and the giver is Εὐφήτης (Euphetes). ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock phrase, here for a lesser king. οἱ is Phyleus, and ἔδωκεν is the aorist of δίδωμι ‘gave’, which we put as ‘had given’. ἐς πόλεμον φορέειν is ‘to wear into war’ (the epic infinitive in -έειν), and δηΐων ἀνδρῶν ἀλεωρήν is ‘a defence from hostile men’ (ἀλεωρή ‘defence’, δήϊος ‘hostile’).

sentences.t: ὅς οἱ καὶ τότε παιδὸς ἀπὸ χροὸς ἤρκεσ’ ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr: hos hoi kai tote paidos apo chroos ērkes’ olethron.
sentences.l: which for him also then from his son’s skin warded off destruction.
sentences.i: and then too it warded off destruction from his son’s body.
sentences.n: ὅς is masculine, ‘which’, because it refers to θώρηξ ‘breastplate’, which is masculine. οἱ is Phyleus, and παιδός ‘his son’ is Meges, so the breastplate his father had been given saves the son. ἀπὸ χροός is ‘from the skin’, ἤρκεσ’ the elided ἤρκεσε ‘warded off’ (as at 529), and ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὲ Μέγης κόρυθος χαλκήρεος ἱπποδασείης
κύμβαχον ἀκρότατον νύξ’ ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι,
sentences.tr:
tou de Megēs korythos chalkēreos hippodaseiēs
kymbachon akrotaton nyx’ encheï oxyoenti,
sentences.l:
And of him Meges, of the helmet bronze-fitted, horse-haired,
the topmost crown stabbed with his sharp spear,
sentences.i: Meges stabbed the very top of his bronze-fitted helmet, thick with horsehair, with his sharp spear,
sentences.n: τοῦ is Dolops, and the sentence takes his helmet, κόρυθος χαλκήρεος ἱπποδασείης ‘bronze-fitted, thick with horsehair’, in the genitive. κύμβαχον ἀκρότατον is ‘the very top’ (κύμβαχος is a rare word; elsewhere in the Iliad it means ‘head down’ and here it is the top of the helmet, the sense not certain). νύξ’ is the unaugmented aorist νύξε, elided, of νύσσω ‘stab’, and ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι ‘with his sharp spear’.

sentences.t:
ῥῆξε δ’ ἀφ’ ἵππειον λόφον αὐτοῦ· πᾶς δὲ χαμᾶζε
κάππεσεν ἐν κονίῃσι νέον φοίνικι φαεινός.
sentences.tr:
rhēxe d’ aph’ hippeion lophon autou· pas de chamaze
kappesen en koniēisi neon phoiniki phaeinos.
sentences.l:
and broke off from it the horse crest; and the whole of it to the ground
fell down in the dust, newly shining with crimson.
sentences.i: and broke off the horsehair crest from it; and the whole crest fell to the ground in the dust, bright with fresh crimson.
sentences.n: ῥῆξε δ’ ἀφ’ is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’ with ἀπό ‘off’ detached from it (tmesis). ἵππειον λόφον is ‘the crest of horsehair’, αὐτοῦ ‘of it’ the helmet, and πᾶς ‘the whole of it’ the crest. κάππεσεν is κατ- with the unaugmented πέσεν, the τ assimilated to the π, ‘fell down’; χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’, and ἐν κονίῃσι ‘in the dust’ (κονίη in the epic plural). νέον is ‘newly’, φοίνικι ‘with crimson’ (the dye φοῖνιξ), and φαεινός ‘shining’: a crest freshly dyed.

sentences.t:
εἷος ὃ τῷ πολέμιζε μένων, ἔτι δ’ ἔλπετο νίκην,
τόφρα δέ οἱ Μενέλαος ἀρήϊος ἦλθεν ἀμύντωρ,
sentences.tr:
heios ho tōi polemize menōn, eti d’ elpeto nikēn,
tophra de hoi Menelaos arēïos ēlthen amyntōr,
sentences.l:
As long as he was fighting him, standing firm, and still hoped for victory,
meanwhile to him came warlike Menelaus, as defender,
sentences.i: While Dolops stood firm and fought Meges, still hoping for victory, warlike Menelaus came to Meges as a defender,
sentences.n: εἷος (Attic ἕως) is ‘while’, answered by τόφρα ‘meanwhile’. ὃ is Dolops, and τῷ and οἱ are Meges, who is the man fighting and the man defended. πολέμιζε is the imperfect of πολεμίζω ‘fight’, μένων ‘standing firm’, and ἔλπετο the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hoped’. ἀρήϊος Μενέλαος is ‘warlike Menelaus’, and ἀμύντωρ ‘defender’ is in apposition to him.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ εὐρὰξ σὺν δουρὶ λαθών, βάλε δ’ ὦμον ὄπισθεν·
sentences.tr: stē d’ eurax syn douri lathōn, bale d’ ōmon opisthen·
sentences.l: and he stood sideways with his spear, unnoticed, and hit him on the shoulder from behind;
sentences.i: He took his stand to one side with his spear, unseen, and hit Dolops on the shoulder from behind;
sentences.n: The subject is Menelaus. στῆ is the root aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’, and εὐράξ is a rare word, usually explained as ‘sideways’; the exact stance is not clear. λαθών is the aorist participle of λανθάνω ‘escaping notice’, βάλε the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’, ὦμον ‘on the shoulder’ and ὄπισθεν ‘from behind’.

sentences.t:
αἰχμὴ δὲ στέρνοιο διέσσυτο μαιμώωσα
πρόσσω ἱεμένη· ὃ δ’ ἄρα πρηνὴς ἐλιάσθη.
sentences.tr:
aichmē de sternoio diessyto maimōōsa
prossō hiemenē· ho d’ ara prēnēs eliasthē.
sentences.l:
and the spear-point through the chest rushed through, raging,
pressing forward; and he then face-forward bent down.
sentences.i: and the spear-point, raging, rushed through his chest, pressing forward; and Dolops sank down on his face.
sentences.n: αἰχμή is the spear-point, and στέρνοιο the epic genitive of στέρνον ‘chest’, ‘through the chest’. διέσσυτο is the aorist of διασεύομαι ‘rush through’, μαιμώωσα the feminine participle of μαιμάω ‘rage’, the spear being as eager as the man who threw it, and ἱεμένη the participle of ἵεμαι ‘press on’; πρόσσω is ‘forward’. ὃ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and he then’, πρηνής ‘face forward’, and ἐλιάσθη the aorist passive of λιάζομαι ‘bend, sink down’ (the verb of 520, there ‘swerve’).

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἐεισάσθην χαλκήρεα τεύχε’ ἀπ’ ὤμων
συλήσειν·
sentences.tr:
tō men eeisasthēn chalkērea teuche’ ap’ ōmōn
sylēsein·
sentences.l:
The two rushed, the bronze-fitted armour from his shoulders
to strip;
sentences.i: The two of them rushed to strip the bronze-fitted armour from his shoulders;
sentences.n: τὼ μέν is the dual, ‘the two’, Meges and Menelaus. ἐεισάσθην is a dual past form of a verb meaning ‘rush’ (related to ἵεμαι ‘hasten’), and συλήσειν the future infinitive of συλάω ‘strip’, which gives the purpose. χαλκήρεα τεύχε’ ἀπ’ ὤμων is ‘the bronze-fitted armour from his shoulders’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ κασιγνήτοισι κέλευσε
πᾶσι μάλα, πρῶτον δ’ Ἱκεταονίδην ἐνένιπεν
ἴφθιμον Μελάνιππον.
sentences.tr:
Hektōr de kasignētoisi keleuse
pasi mala, prōton d’ Hiketaonidēn enenipen
iphthimon Melanippon.
sentences.l:
and Hector to his brothers gave orders,
to all of them, and first Hicetaon’s-son he rebuked,
mighty Melanippus.
sentences.i: But Hector gave orders to all his brothers, every one, and first of all rebuked the son of Hicetaon, mighty Melanippus.
sentences.n: Ἕκτωρ δέ turns the story to the Trojan side. κασιγνήτοισι is ‘to his brothers’, the dative plural of κασίγνητος; the word can reach to near kin generally, and the men are not named. πᾶσι μάλα is ‘to all of them, every one’, and πρῶτον ‘first’. Ἱκεταονίδην is the patronymic of Ἱκετάων, ‘Hicetaon’s son’, and ἐνένιπεν is the aorist of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’ with its reduplicated stem. ἴφθιμον ‘mighty’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὄφρα μὲν εἰλίποδας βοῦς
βόσκ’ ἐν Περκώτῃ δηΐων ἀπὸ νόσφιν ἐόντων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ophra men eilipodas bous
bosk’ en Perkōtēi dēïōn apo nosphin eontōn·
sentences.l:
And he, so long as the rolling-gaited cattle
he was grazing at Percote, the enemy being far away;
sentences.i: As long as the enemy were far away, he was grazing his cattle of rolling gait at Percote;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Melanippus, and ὄφρα μέν ‘so long as’ is answered by αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ‘but when’ in the next line. βόσκ’ is the unaugmented imperfect βόσκε, elided, of βόσκω ‘graze’. εἰλίποδας βοῦς is ‘cattle of rolling gait’ (εἰλίπους, said of the heavy walk of cattle). ἐν Περκώτῃ is ‘at Percote’ (Περκώτη, a town in the Troad). δηΐων ἀπὸ νόσφιν ἐόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘the enemy being far away’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Δαναῶν νέες ἤλυθον ἀμφιέλισσαι,
sentences.tr: autar epei Danaōn nees ēlython amphielissai,
sentences.l: but when the ships of the Danaans came, both-sides-curving,
sentences.i: but when the Danaans’ ships, curved on both sides, came,
sentences.n: ἤλυθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι ‘came’, and ἀμφιέλισσαι ‘curved on both sides’ is the stock epithet of ships; the sense is disputed. The line stands unchanged at 13.174.

sentences.t:
ἂψ εἰς Ἴλιον ἦλθε, μετέπρεπε δὲ Τρώεσσι,
ναῖε δὲ πὰρ Πριάμῳ, ὃ δέ μιν τίεν ἶσα τέκεσσι·
sentences.tr:
aps eis Ilion ēlthe, meteprepe de Trōessi,
naie de par Priamōi, ho de min tien isa tekessi·
sentences.l:
back to Ilios he came, and was conspicuous among the Trojans,
and lived beside Priam, and he honoured him equally with his children;
sentences.i: he came back to Ilios and was conspicuous among the Trojans, and lived beside Priam, who honoured him equally with his children;
sentences.n: ἂψ εἰς Ἴλιον is ‘back to Ilios’, and μετέπρεπε the imperfect of μεταπρέπω ‘be conspicuous among’. ναῖε is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, πὰρ Πριάμῳ ‘beside Priam’, and ὃ δέ μιν τίεν ἶσα τέκεσσι ‘and he honoured him equally with his children’, with τίεν the imperfect of τίω ‘honour’ and τέκεσσι the epic dative plural of τέκος ‘child’. The two lines are those of 13.175–176, with εἰς here for the ἐς there and a comma after Πριάμῳ where 13.176 has a stop.

sentences.t: τόν ῥ’ Ἕκτωρ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr: ton rh’ Hektōr enenipen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l: Him then Hector rebuked, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: Hector rebuked him, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: τόν ῥ’ is ‘him then’, ῥ’ being ῥα, and ἐνένιπεν is the verb of line 546. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is a stock half-line: ἔφατ’ is the imperfect ‘spoke’ and ἐκ … ὀνόμαζεν (tmesis) ‘called by name’. The speech follows.

sentences.t:
οὕτω δὴ Μελάνιππε μεθήσομεν; οὐδέ νυ σοί περ
ἐντρέπεται φίλον ἦτορ ἀνεψιοῦ κταμένοιο;
sentences.tr:
houtō dē Melanippe methēsomen; oude ny soi per
entrepetai philon ētor anepsiou ktamenoio;
sentences.l:
“Is it thus indeed, Melanippus, that we shall slacken? And not even in you
does your dear heart heed your slain cousin?
sentences.i: “Are we to slacken like this, Melanippus? Does not even your own heart heed your cousin, who has been killed?
sentences.n: Hector speaks, and the question is bitter. οὕτω δή is ‘so then’, and μεθήσομεν the first plural future of μεθίημι ‘let go, slacken’, here a deliberative ‘are we to …?’ with no object stated. οὐδέ νυ … περ is ‘and not even’, σοί ‘in you’, and ἐντρέπεται ‘heeds’, taking the genitive ἀνεψιοῦ κταμένοιο, ‘your slain cousin’ (ἀνεψιός ‘cousin’, κταμένοιο the epic genitive of the root-aorist participle of κτείνω, middle in form and passive in sense). The cousin is Dolops, as the next line shows.

sentences.t: οὐχ ὁράᾳς οἷον Δόλοπος περὶ τεύχε’ ἕπουσιν;
sentences.tr: ouch horaāis hoion Dolopos peri teuche’ hepousin;
sentences.l: Do you not see how they are busy about Dolops’ armour?
sentences.i: Do you not see how they are busy over Dolops’ armour?
sentences.n: ὁράᾳς is the second singular of ὁράω with the Homeric open spelling. οἷον is ‘how’, introducing what Melanippus is to see, and Δόλοπος is the genitive of Δόλοψ. ἕπουσιν is the third plural of ἕπω ‘be busy about’, with περὶ τεύχε’ ‘about the armour’: the Achaeans are stripping Dolops.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἕπευ·
sentences.tr: all’ hepeu·
sentences.l: But follow;
sentences.i: But follow me;
sentences.n: ἕπευ is the imperative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ (epic -ευ, Attic ἕπου), the middle of the verb whose active ἕπουσιν is in the last line.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἔστιν ἀποσταδὸν Ἀργείοισι
μάρνασθαι, πρίν γ’ ἠὲ κατακτάμεν ἠὲ κατ’ ἄκρης
Ἴλιον αἰπεινὴν ἑλέειν κτάσθαι τε πολίτας.
sentences.tr:
ou gar et’ estin apostadon Argeioisi
marnasthai, prin g’ ēe kataktamen ēe kat’ akrēs
Ilion aipeinēn heleein ktasthai te politas.
sentences.i: for it is no longer possible to fight the Argives from a distance, until we have either killed them or steep Ilios has been taken from top to bottom and its citizens killed.”
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἔστιν is ‘for it is no longer possible’, ἀποσταδόν ‘standing apart, at a distance’, and μάρνασθαι ‘to fight’ with Ἀργείοισι in the dative, ‘against the Argives’. πρίν γ’ is ‘before’ with infinitives, and ἠέ … ἠέ ‘either … or’; κατακτάμεν is the aorist infinitive of κατακτείνω ‘kill’. ἑλέειν is the epic aorist infinitive of αἱρέω ‘take’, Ἴλιον αἰπεινήν ‘steep Ilios’, and κατ’ ἄκρης ‘from the top down’. κτάσθαι is the root-aorist middle infinitive of κτείνω (cf. κταμένοιο at 553), passive in sense, ‘be killed’. The Greek leaves the subjects unsaid, and the English supplies them; ἑλέειν is an active infinitive, and the English puts it as ‘has been taken’ beside the passive κτάσθαι. The speech, and the part, end here.
